items.summary: India has rejected the United States' assertion that it possesses structural excess capacity in any sector, even as New Delhi faces the prospect of higher tariffs if trade negotiations fail. The U.S. cited excess capacity while proposing fresh tariffs on 14 economies (q1). Washington proposed capping tariffs on Indian imports at 17 per cent (q2) if an agreement is reached, with the rate potentially rising to 25 per cent (q3) if no deal materializes.
items.title: India Rejects US Excess Capacity Claim Amid Tariff Negotiations

items.summary: Indian retail investors sold equities worth around ₹24,953 crore so far in November, their highest-ever selling since the National Stock Exchange began publishing this data in October 2023. A detailed break-up of their primary and secondary-market transactions for November is not available. Despite that recent selling, retail investors remained net buyers of ₹41,600 crore so far in 2026. Shrikant Chouhan, head of equity research at Kotak Neo, said domestic institutions had absorbed substantial foreign selling over the past two years when the Nifty was trading around 22,000-23,000.
items.title: Retail investors turned net sellers in November as FIIs piled into Indian stocks

items.summary: In June, Flo Crivello moved all of the AI work at his San Francisco startup Lindy off Anthropic's Claude and onto cheaper models from DeepSeek, a Chinese company that lets anyone download its software and run it. The roughly 25-person company had been paying "unsustainable" AI bills for a long time, according to Crivello, who told CNBC the switch was "a matter of survival for the business." After moving away from Claude, he said the cost curve dropped sharply, like it "crashed to the ground," and expects the move to save Lindy millions of dollars within months. However, even after this reduction in AI costs, Crivello noted that the startup will still spend more on AI than on its payroll.
items.title: Businesses Switching from Claude to Cheaper Free AI Models

items.summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi greeted citizens on Thursday's Constitution Day, honoring Dr B.R. Ambedkar and other members of the Constituent Assembly for their role in framing India's Constitution. In his remarks, Modi stated that 'for crores of Indians, including me, the Constitution of India is an inseparable part of our life journeys,' underscoring its significance to the nation.
items.title: Modi Pays Tribute to Ambedkar on Constitution Day

items.summary: India has rejected U.S. claims that it possesses structural excess capacity in manufacturing, responding to a Notice of Determination and Request for Comments issued by the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) under its Section 301 investigation into 14 economies — including India — on acts, policies, and practices relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors; the Commerce Ministry stated that
items.title: India Rejects US Excess Capacity Claims Amid Threat of 25% Tariffs

items.summary: An IBM report, Proof, Not Promises: The Digital Sovereignty Index, finds that Indian organizations achieved the highest overall Digital Sovereignty Index score among surveyed markets at 79.0 out of 100 versus a global average of 74.0 (IBM). At the same time, India reported substantial barriers when sovereignty was tested, with an average significant-barrier level of 61% versus 51% globally (IBM). The report notes that while 88% of Indian organizations express high confidence in demonstrating sovereign control, only 35% meet the Index's 'Leading' evidence maturity threshold — still the highest share among surveyed markets but revealing a gap between perceived readiness and demonstrated evidence. India also leads on testing behavior: 45% test sovereignty continuously or as part of regular governance processes versus 33% globally (IBM). The study defines digital sovereignty as an organization's ability to retain control and provide credible evidence across critical AI, technology, operations and data; 70% of Indian respondents said this definition closely aligned with their organizations' understanding. In practice, 97% of Indian organizations experienced at least one situation testing their digital sovereignty in the preceding three years versus 94% globally (IBM), and among those affected, 90% required formal evidence of control as part of an external request or internal review versus 81% globally.
items.title: IBM Survey Finds India Leads Digital Sovereignty Index but Faces Barriers

items.summary: An analysis of Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) examination statistics registration data, accessed by The Times of India (TOI), shows the gap between chemistry and business studies candidates has more than doubled — from 2.9 lakh in 2019 to 6.3 lakh as reported for 2027. Over eight years, candidate numbers grew roughly 70 percent in chemistry, nearly 58 percent in physics, about 55 percent in mathematics, and around 32 percent each in business studies and accountancy, indicating a widening science-versus-commerce divide among CBSE students.
items.title: Chemistry Becomes CBSE's Most Popular Subject After English

items.summary: If elected, a Victorian Coalition government led by opposition leader Jess Wilson would privatise two sewage treatment plants as part of a $14.47bn 'asset recycling' plan announced during the Liberal-National pre-election policy costings on Thursday. The plan includes a sale of state land to developers and a $9.2bn, 90-year lease of the Eastern and Western treatment plants that process most of Melbourne's sewage, with Wilson stating there would be no change to water bills as a result. It also involves selling air rights between Richmond train station and the MCG on the condition the station is revitalised, having renewable energy buyers purchase State Electricity Commission assets recently revived by Labor, plus $5.73bn in savings from drawing down contingencies and $1.23bn from reprioritising level crossing removals. The independent Parliamentary Budget Office found the plan would lower net debt to $176bn by 2029-30, compared with $196bn outlined in Treasury's pre-election budget update this month, saving the state $4.2bn in interest payments.
items.title: Victorian Coalition's $14.47bn Asset Recycling Plan Would Privatise Sewage Plants and Sell State Assets

items.summary: The UK government is set to publish on Thursday afternoon the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a new deal with the EU, along with legislation to enact most of it. The BBC reports that the treaties include a 10-year termination clause requiring any party ending the agreement within that period to pay for rebuilding border-checks infrastructure being scaled back under the deal; opposition figures Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage have suggested they would refuse to fund such payments. The Brexit reset deal covers British food exports, emissions trading, and a youth experience scheme, with two of three legal texts addressing food trade and an emissions trading agreement alongside a government cost-cutting bill. The treaties will affect the UK aviation and maritime industries through alignment with EU emissions schemes, and new sectoral and regional impact assessments are expected. Food exporters stand to benefit from reduced red tape and dismantled border facilities, with an internal analysis forecasting a 16% boost to agricultural exports, though industry insiders privately told the BBC that global economic factors—including energy price shocks linked to war in the Middle East—may limit visible cost savings for consumers. European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said the Cutting Costs Bill enables two major trade agreements while eliminating paperwork for food and drink traders and protecting British exports from carbon taxes. The legislation will detail how the UK will observe and shape but not vote on EU rules, including granting ministers direct 'Henry VIII powers' to align UK and EU laws through secondary legislation. Prime Minister Andy Burnham described new EU agreements as pragmatic rather than a prelude to further action, stating it would be unthinkable for the UK to rejoin without a referendum; several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen Brexit debates. Badenoch countered that Burnham has oversold the deal and is attempting to return Britain to 2015.
items.title: UK Set to Publish Brexit Reset Treaties with EU

items.summary: An out-of-control bushfire in northern Tasmania's Flinders Island destroyed or damaged at least six properties and forced residents to shelter as smoke blanketed the island. By Thursday midday, the fire — characterized by 10-metre-high flames — had burned through approximately 14,500 hectares, roughly 10% of the island, with authorities warning more homes were at risk. Northern TFS deputy regional chief Steve Richardson said the fire front was making a significant run toward the south-west after Wednesday's horrendous conditions made direct firefighting unsafe in some areas; nearly 40 firefighters plus 12 parks and wildlife staff, five helicopters and three aircraft (with nine additional vehicles arriving Thursday) were working to control it. Emergency services warned residents of Killicrankie that evacuation routes were threatened and told them to enact bushfire plans, shelter with clear exits, bring pets inside, close doors and windows, or use Killiecrankie beach as a last resort — while communities in Leeka, Mt Tanner, Mt Boyes and Carnacs Flat were warned it was unsafe to return. Flinders Island is about 130,000 hectares of land home to roughly 900 people. Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff announced government emergency assistance grants opening from 2pm Thursday for those who had to relocate — $250 per adult and $125 per child, capped at a maximum of $1,000 per family.
items.title: Out-of-control bushfire with 10-metre flames destroys at least six homes on Flinders Island

items.summary: The Trump administration is proposing new tariffs targeting China, the European Union, and a dozen other trading partners it says have distorted global markets by overproducing goods such as automobiles, batteries, and chemicals. These so-called excess capacity tariffs conclude investigations that began in March, comply with existing trade deals, and vary by country. A senior US official said the administration is suggesting a 20% 'across the board' tariff on Chinese exports (reading q1), which would stack with 2018 tariffs but not 2026 forced-labor tariffs and exempt goods identified by the Board of Trade; that rate could rise as high as 40% if trade talks collapse. The official said China is unlikely to retaliate beyond a statement, while expecting more agreements at next month's G20 summit in its wake. The announcement follows exit polling finding eight in 10 voters believe Trump's tariffs have harmed the economy (reading q5), and comes amid scrutiny of US-China policy following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Officials predicted the proposed tariffs could take effect in January at the earliest, after soliciting comments and holding hearings, while investigations into Norway and Mexico remain ongoing; on the same night the administration also proposed new tariffs on Brazilian sugar and aircraft over a 'lack of progress' in trade talks.
items.title: US Proposes Sweeping New Tariffs on China and Other Trading Partners

items.summary: On the first anniversary of Hong Kong's deadly Tai Po fire, CNA reports that displaced residents and schoolchildren remain struggling to rebuild their lives. The fire broke out on Nov 26, 2025 (d3), killing 168 people in what was described as Hong Kong's deadliest blaze in decades (q4). A year later, survivors including Athena Kwong and Marco Chan, both 29, remain living in temporary accommodation — a 12sqm unit at a transitional housing facility with limited space for everyday comforts (q2) — while awaiting permanent homes. Although their apartment was not directly affected by the fire, they will never return to it because the government plans to demolish Wang Fuk Court; the couple has purchased a flat in Fanling through a special sales exercise but does not want to settle there. The government offered displaced residents subsidised flats in several locations, some of which will not be ready until 2031 (d5). At Tai Po Baptist Public School, which stood opposite Wang Fuk Court and had to vacate its campus for emergency relief efforts, students were split between two temporary sites before moving into a renovated campus at Fu Shin Estate in September. Among the students are 30 children who lived at Wang Fuk Court (q6), some of whom still cope with trauma from witnessing the fire — social worker Dawn Leung noted that affected students can be triggered by everyday sounds and bright lights, requiring careful handling even during routine fire drills.
items.title: Hong Kong Tai Po fire survivors still rebuilding a year after deadliest blaze

items.summary: Australian business investment surged in the September quarter, driven by record data centre spending and reaching its highest level since 2011 during the mining boom. The Australian Bureau of Statistics reported private capital spending jumped 12.2 per cent to an inflation-adjusted A$59.5 billion ($39.37 billion), far above market forecasts of a 4.4 per cent rise. This was led by an 87 per cent jump in spending on information media and telecommunications equipment, reflecting record investment in server racks and processing gear for data centres — much of it imported equipment that offset economic growth. Overall plant and machinery spending rose 23.1 per cent while buildings and structures increased 1.7 per cent. Abhijit Surya of Capital Economics noted ICT capital spending could nearly double in the 2027 financial year, contrasting with a struggling broader economy. The strong figures suggested some economic resilience despite five interest rate hikes this year that triggered Australia's worst housing downturn in 40 years and weakened consumer spending and the labour market.
items.title: Data Centre Investment Drives Australia's Biggest Business Spending Rise Since the Mining Boom

items.summary: On November 26, Brent crude traded at $94.66 per barrel around 7:30 am after briefly falling below $90 earlier in the week and ending just under $95 on Wednesday; WTI hovered near $84 a barrel following more than 4% gains over two sessions. The rebound followed attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura export hub, along with Iranian claims that vessels crossing the Strait of Hormuz struck mines and that two tankers hit naval mines after taking an unauthorized route. Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $105 a barrel from $90 previously and lifted its WTI projection to $94 from $81; in a more bullish scenario, it warned Brent could reach $140 a barrel by 2027 if Gulf oil production stays about 3.5 million barrels per day below the 2025 average. JPMorgan similarly cautioned that markets remain caught between supply-disruption risks and offsetting capacity while noting several economic thresholds have been breached seven months into the conflict.
items.title: Brent crude rose to $94.66 as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia renewed supply fears

items.summary: The Bank of Korea resumed monetary tightening by raising its seven-day repurchase rate to the highest level since November 2024, marking the third increase this year and bringing cumulative policy-rate hikes to 75 basis points. The vote followed back-to-back increases in July and August, with a decision forecast by 32 of 34 analysts surveyed by Reuters. Governor Shin Hyun Song is scheduled to hold a news conference at 0210 GMT to explain the board's decision and present updated projections; she has said last month that the bank will take a data-dependent approach rather than follow a fixed rate trajectory. The central bank raised its growth forecast for this year to 3.9% from 3.3%, while projecting a 4.1% expansion next year, up from 2.9%. A projected 4.1% growth would be the fastest since 2021, when the economy grew 4.7%, driven by surging global demand for semiconductors in what is Asia's fourth-largest economy. The bank also raised its inflation outlook to 2.4% for 2027 from 2.3%. Policymakers maintained a hawkish stance amid a heated housing market and headline inflation near 3%, well above the BOK's 2% target.
items.title: South Korea's central bank resumes tightening with quarter-point hike

items.summary: In Terengganu, Malaysia, a community-led conservation program run by the Turtle Conservation Society of Malaysia (TCS) has transformed former river terrapin egg harvesters into night-time nest guardians. Since 2011, TCS data shows these Terrapin Guardians have collected and incubated more than 13,000 eggs — with a specific figure cited at 13,224 — and released more than 8,200 young terrapins back into the river. The southern river terrapin (Batagur affinis) is listed as critically endangered on the IUCN Red List, with most of its remaining wild population found in Peninsular Malaysia; all freshwater turtles and tortoises were declared fully protected under Malaysia's Wildlife Conservation Act in 2010. During nesting season from January to March, a team of 13 guardians — including former collectors like Samsul bin Hamid — work nights along the Kemaman River tracking nests, weighing, measuring, microchipping and incubating eggs at TCS hatchery for three months before releasing the hatchlings. Chen Pelf Nyok, co-founder and executive director of TCS, explains that terrapin egg collecting was traditionally shared among neighbors rather than sold: a typical clutch of 35 eggs could be split among up to 10 people, yielding roughly 24–40 ringgit ($6–$10) even at 8–10 ringgit per egg — far less than the 350–500 ringgit ($86–$123) a trader could earn from a single clutch of green turtle eggs. Despite these efforts, terrapins remain threatened by natural predators such as monitor lizards and by sand mining that destroys nesting sandbanks; TCS currently monitors six sandbanks along the river and hopes they can be formally protected. Experts note that community-based programs matter most for their lasting social impact on how local communities value a species.
items.title: Former egg collectors in Terengganu now guard Malaysia's critically endangered river terrapins

items.summary: Asian stocks fell sharply along with lower US futures as investors grew increasingly worried about a potential technology sector downturn, compounded by reports that the Washington administration plans to impose new tariffs on more than a dozen trading partners, potentially including China, the EU, and Japan. One investor told CNBC that bond markets are demanding stronger evidence that Big Tech's large capital expenditure plans will translate into higher revenues. Separately, US President Donald Trump is reportedly set to announce an additional round of duties on imports from over a dozen countries. The market volatility has prompted some analysts to draw parallels with the late-2018 selloff; at that time, Citadel's head of macro strategy noted that the strength of the US economy was insufficient to offset broader economic concerns.
items.title: Asian Stocks and US Futures Fall on Tariff Fears and Tech Bust Concerns

items.summary: A survey compiled by the Japanese trade promotion agency JETRO, conducted from August to September this year and received responses from 7,695 companies, found that Chinese firms are becoming more competitive with Japanese firms operating abroad. The number of respondents who said there were more competitors in general than two years earlier rose to 38 per cent. Respondents identified Chinese firms as the largest sources of competition in Central and South America, Africa and Thailand, and noted that Chinese firms had become more competitive across most key regions and countries. When asked about Chinese firms' strengths, 97.1 per cent of respondents cited cost competitiveness and 48.1 per cent pointed to speed of decision-making. A US seller of electronic parts attributed the challenge partly to improved product quality alongside low prices, while a German electronics equipment seller said Japanese companies are focusing on high-barrier industries such as air traffic control and defence. JETRO chair Norihiko Ishiguro stated that the selling point of Japanese products is becoming high-value add and safety.
items.title: JETRO Survey Finds Chinese Firms Growing Competitive Threat to Japanese Companies Abroad

items.summary: Spain is holding snap general elections on Sunday, 29 November, after Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez dissolved parliament eight months early following MPs' rejection of housing-law changes. The vote pits continued Socialist-led rule against a likely conservative government under Alberto Núñez Feijóo's People's Party (PP), with the far-right Vox expected to support it; most polls show the PP narrowly ahead of the Socialists, though Feijóo would need Vox backing and has said he will not sign agreements that breach Spain's constitution or EU treaties. The electorate is nearly 39 million people eligible across a country of almost 50 million, with polls open at 09:00 (08:00 GMT) and closing at 20:00 (19:00 GMT), when first exit polls emerge.
items.title: Spain's Snap Election Pits Feijóo Against Sánchez Over Housing and Migration

items.summary: France's political mainstream faces a potential wipe-out at the April-May 2027 presidential election unless it quickly selects a centre-ground candidate, as polls consistently show hard-right leader Marine Le Pen and hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon dominating. The middle ground is being squeezed out because both polarised leaders have more opponents than supporters among their own bases, which should theoretically favour any contender who survives the first round's multi-candidate vote to win a fortnight later in the play-off; however, personal rivalries and differing visions have undermined this hope. On the left, agreement has emerged on candidate Raphaël Glucksmann from the Socialist Party, but his support is being pulled into Mélenchon's orbit as Green leader Marine Tondelier, most Communist parliamentary deputies, Benoît Hamon, and François Ruffin all withdraw or align with France Unbowed (LFI). On the right, once-bright prospects have dimmed: Edouard Philippe's poll ratings fell sharply to place him behind Mélenchon in first-round projections while Le Pen leads both. Other centre-right candidates are circling, including former Macron prime ministers Gabriel Attal and Bruno Retailleau, plus surprise liberal challenger David Lisnard of Nouvelle Energie (New Energy), whose membership has risen above 100,000 as he appeals to voters seeking an alternative to Le Pen on immigration while avoiding her language. Commentators warn the centre-right lacks a coherent strategy: Nicolas Baverez says there is "a total vacuum" in the space between Le Pen and Mélenchon for strategy, programme, and activists, with digital campaigning especially absent compared with both polarised leaders' effective social media efforts; Guillaume Tabard notes that while Le Pen issued pension reform proposals and Mélenchon published a best-selling book, the middle offers only disputes over names, polling figures, and whether to hold a primary. Lisnard's rise is attributed by Fressoz to his right-of-right positioning on immigration, though as an economic liberal he faces a minority taste in France that could deflate him after an initial surge. Optimists hope polls will settle behind one centre-right candidate come the new year with others stepping aside, and talk of a 2017-style primary is ebbing even as Philippe and Lisnard remain opposed; Tabard dismisses support for such a primary from Retailleau and Attal as merely keeping hopes alive. Fressoz concludes that after years of Macron's "neither left nor right," the extremes now control French politics, with Le Pen and Mélenchon—both having run three times, with long-established visions, strategies, trained activists, and polarisation to their advantage—having had the 2027 outcome in sight for years.
items.title: France's political mainstream risks presidential vote debacle with no clear candidate

items.summary: Tasmania's auditor-general Martin Thompson said the messaging around a fuel surcharge imposed by Spirit of Tasmania operator TT-Line was likely to mislead passengers, because the company was actually spending less on fuel. TT-Line had announced in late March that it would impose a 15 per cent surcharge on fares from then until the end of August, citing an
items.title: Tasmania's Auditor-General Says TT-Line Fuel Surcharge Messaging Was Misleading

items.summary: The India Meteorological Department issued a thunderstorm and lightning warning for Chennai on Thursday, November 26, with the alert extending to Friday as well. Bengaluru is expected to see light rain under mostly cloudy skies, while Delhi will experience mist and fog over the weekend along with cooler temperatures—its Safdarjung station forecast at a maximum of 27°C on Thursday, dropping to 25°C on Friday, with minimums holding around 9–10°C. Hyderabad may develop thunder and lightning despite having no formal weather warning for Thursday, while Kolkata is expected to remain mainly clear through the period. Mumbai and Pune will both see mostly clear skies at highs of about 32°C on Thursday; recorded rainfall was zero in both cities as of Wednesday morning, though Mumbai's high could climb to 34°C by Sunday. Ahmedabad should stay mainly clear with a Friday peak around 32°C extending into early December.
items.title: IMD Warns Chennai of Lightning; Forecasts Vary Across Indian Metro Cities

items.summary: During Samvidhan Divas (Constitution Day), Prime Minister Narendra Modi criticized the opposition, accusing Congress of weakening the Indian Constitution over decades and labeling opposition forces 'Dimagi Naxals.' He described the Emergency as a dark period for Indian democracy, highlighted government achievements, and condemned opposition efforts to block women's empowerment bills. The source notes that Constitution Day remains a point of contention among political parties regarding constitutional values.
items.title: Modi Accuses Opposition of Undermining Constitution and Blocking Women Empowerment

items.summary: The lighting of the Karthigai Deepam lamp at Tirupparankundram has become a political and religious dispute in Tamil Nadu, with the matter returning to the Supreme Court after new concerns about submissions made by the Tamil Nadu government. Temple priests contesting the temple trust's account state they did not consent to lighting the lamp at Ucchipillaiyar Temple and never opposed lighting it at Deepathoon, whereas the temple trust asserts that the customary location was chosen with both priestly input and board approval. The Madurai district collector apologized for the Deepam not being lit at Deepathoon and denied any intentional disobedience. BJP State President Nainar Nagendran criticized Chief Minister Vijay over alleged non-compliance with court orders and religious bias during a fresh plea seeking permission for the 11-day ritual.
items.title: Tirupparankundram Deepam Dispute Reaches Supreme Court Amid Questions Over Government Claims

items.summary: The Samajwadi Party (SP) and the Congress are set to hold a second round of seat-sharing talks for next year's Uttar Pradesh assembly elections on Friday, days after the SP's first candidate list triggered friction in the alliance. The two allies are expected to complete seat-by-seat discussions over all 403 seats in the state, with the Congress demanding more than the 26 offered by the regional party and far exceeding its earlier demand of at least 50 winnable seats on the first day of negotiations that lasted less than 20 minutes. The SP's opening offer of 26 seats was much lower than the national party's initial request for 181 assembly constituencies, which it had sought as part of the SP-led alliance in a November 14 Hindustan Times Leadership Summit address by SP chief Akhilesh Yadav.
items.title: SP, Congress to hold second round of UP seat-sharing talks amid alliance friction

items.summary: Three days before India's second Test at Hagley Oval in Christchurch, the BCCI media team issued a terse WhatsApp alert confirming no practice and no press conference. With only a three-day turnaround between Tests after bowling 241 combined overs across two innings at the Basin Reserve, India will have just one training session on Thursday as they focus on recovery, selection and execution. The article centres on whether India should repeat their pace-heavy attack of Jasprit Bumrah, Akash Deep, Prasidh Krishna and Anshul Kamboj or make changes in the bowling department. Bumrah bowled 49 overs at Basin while Kamboj and Prasidh each bowled 45 and Akash 43. At Basin, skipper Shubman Gill hinted India may not tinker much with their combination, a stance supported by venue history: across the 15 men's Tests played there, pacers took 444 of the 484 wickets — 91.7%. Selection questions include whether Gurnoor Brar could replace Anshul Kamboj after being named Player of the Series in the ODIs and added to the Test squad, or whether Mohammed Siraj should return for Akash Deep given India's record that Siraj has featured significantly in all nine Tests won by India in SENA countries since 2020. The current regime under Gill and coach Gautam Gambhir prioritises current form and net eye tests rather than such historical arguments. Hagley is also known to reward seam, with a forecast of sunshine over the first three days but more cloud and rain on Days Four and Five — which could make fresh pace legs important if India bowl first after winning the toss.
items.title: India face selection dilemma ahead of second Test against New Zealand

items.summary: The Delhi Police has refused permission for a march by the Students' Kidney Movement (SKM) to Jantar Mantar, which was scheduled to coincide with the anniversary of the farmers' protest. The denial prevents the group from proceeding with its planned demonstration at that location and date.
items.title: Delhi Police Denies SKM Permission to March to Jantar Mantar on Farmers' Protest Anniversary

items.summary: A fuel tanker crash that ignited a massive fire on Egypt's Ring Road, which encircles the capital of Cairo, killed at least 31 people and injured at least 21, Egyptian authorities reported. The incident occurred Wednesday in Waraq, a densely populated neighborhood in Giza within Greater Cairo (the article also references nearby Imbaba), where rescue workers pulled survivors from burning cars and more than two dozen vehicles were left charred. President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi issued condolences to the victims while DNA investigations began to identify them; Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said injured people had been taken to hospitals, noting that death toll figures remained preliminary and could rise further.
items.title: Fuel Tanker Crash on Cairo's Ring Road Kills at Least 31

items.summary: Vedat Muriqi scored the second-half winner as Fenerbahce beat Shakhtar Donetsk 1-0 at London's Stamford Bridge in the fifth matchday of the UEFA Champions League league phase, held on Wednesday (26 November 2026). An early goal by Muriqi in the 18th minute was disallowed after a VAR review for a foul on Shakhtar captain Mykola Matviienko. Fenerbahce came close again when goalkeeper Dmytro Riznyk made a fingertip save to deny Oguz Aydin's effort toward the bottom corner in the 41st minute, and Muriqi broke the deadlock by tapping home a rebound after Riznyk saved Mason Greenwood's shot in the 56th minute. Substitute Romelu Lukaku missed a stoppage-time one-on-one opportunity in the 92nd minute as Shakhtar failed to equalize. The victory marked Fenerbahce's first away win in the Champions League proper in 22 years, since defeating Sparta Prague in November 2004 (November 2004). It lifted them to 16th place with eight points from five matches, while Shakhtar dropped to 26th on four points.
items.title: Fenerbahce beats Shakhtar Donetsk 1-0 to end a Champions League away win drought

items.summary: Big technology firms tied to artificial intelligence saw share prices fall on Wednesday, with Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading. The surge in Nvidia shares after CEO Jensen Huang was reinstated proved temporary; the stock fell 8% in early trading before ending 3.4% lower at close as a broad sell-off continued across all three main US indices. Concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment rattled investors, who also took fright at Democrat gains in the midterm elections amid campaigns for tougher regulation of AI firms and even a moratorium on new data centres. Nvidia's rocky fortnight had wider impact given its role as both supplier and financier to other AI companies. Amazon shares fell just over 3%, while Anthropic traded below its $83 debut price; Meta and SpaceX were positive by close, though the Nasdaq closed 0.6% lower. The declines came alongside a raft of new tariffs announced Wednesday under President Trump's trade policy, even as big tech has historically sheltered the US economy from global shocks.
items.title: US Stocks Fall as AI Investment Fears Intensify

visual.alt: Bar chart. Nvidia early trading 8 %; Nvidia at close 3.4 %.

items.summary: A Capital Beat panel of analysts debated whether the formal reuniting of the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) and BJP ahead of the 2027 Punjab Assembly elections can revive two parties weakened by past setbacks. Political analyst Jagdeep S Sindhu said the alliance stems from mutual political compulsion rather than ideological convergence, noting that both sides saw it as a way to strengthen their electoral chances; he added that SAD could no longer replicate its earlier results amid fragmentation of the Panthic vote and that BJP abandoned its goal of contesting all 117 seats on its own. Analyst Akash Deep said the alliance's significance should not be read as electoral inevitability, pointing out that the combine's performance declined from 68 seats in 2012 to 18 in 2017 and only five seats when the parties contested separately in 2022; he also flagged lingering controversies for both parties. Deep questioned AAP's governance record, contrasting its promise of 25 lakh jobs with official figures showing around 65,000-75,000 delivered. BJP leader Alok Vats agreed neither party could win alone and that no side holds a decisive edge, while Congress advocate Sanjeet Kumar disputed claims of disunity and criticized AAP over Punjab's debt and revenue deficit. AAP spokesperson Ranbir Singh Dhindsa defended its record—citing free electricity, recruitment drives, toll-plaza closures and pension reforms—and said the SAD-BJP alliance had been losing support since 2015; he also repeated a claim that only 75,000 jobs were delivered without corruption. Sindhu left the 2027 outcome open, saying voter sentiment remains fluid and it is too early to predict either a clear majority or a hung assembly.
items.title: Can the SAD-BJP reunion shift Punjab's electoral balance?

items.summary: External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar paid tribute to those killed in the November 26, 2008 attacks on Mumbai — commonly called 26/11 or '11 Mumbai' — while reaffirming India's zero-tolerance stance toward terrorism. The coordinated assault by a group of 10 Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorists entered the city via sea route and over four days killed 166 people and injured 300, targeting sites such as the Taj and Oberoi Hotels, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, Nariman House, Cama Hospital, Metro Cinema, and Leopold Cafe. Jaishankar saluted the security personnel who died in the attack; nine terrorists were killed during the operation while lone survivor Mohammad Ajmal Amir Kasab was arrested, awarded the death penalty in May 2010, and hanged two years later at a maximum-security prison in Pune.
items.title: Jaishankar Marks 18 Years of the 26/11 Mumbai Attacks and Reaffirms Zero-Tolerance on Terrorism

items.summary: Senior Superintendent of Police Aditya Bansal in Uttar Pradesh's Aligarh reported that police arrested 12 Bangladeshi nationals for allegedly entering India illegally, acting on confidential information. During questioning the individuals reportedly admitted to their illegal entry. Police recovered Aadhaar cards, PAN cards, voter ID cards, bank savings account records and Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) cards from them, along with mobile phones whose examination revealed calls and messages exchanged with relatives in Bangladesh. A case has been registered against all 12 individuals under relevant legal sections, with further investigation underway.
items.title: Aligarh Police Arrest 12 Bangladeshis Over Alleged Illegal Entry

items.summary: Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting more than 10,000 jobs at risk in devastating news for staff just before Christmas. Administrators AlixPartners have been appointed by Poundland's directors after its owner Gordon Brothers rejected bids and declined to provide further funds, with the sales process reportedly failing to identify a viable solvent solution for the business as a whole. The retailer has 600 stores across the UK and Ireland and employed more than 10,000 people — about 2,000 fewer than a month earlier — though it is suggested that up to 30,000 jobs in total could be at risk across its stores, supply chain, and affected high street businesses. Poundland would continue trading while administrators pursue all options, including selling the business or assets in whole or part; about 2,000 suppliers are expected to lose significant business and millions of pounds in payments for stock already supplied. The company was bought by Gordon Brothers from Pepco last year for a nominal £1, took on £30m in shareholder debts at that time, and has faced years of instability amid high inflation and competition; documents provided to MPs show the finance firm had taken close to £20m in interest payments and fees since acquiring Poundland. Founded with one store in Burton upon Trent in 1990, the chain is now expected to be broken up into parcels for retailers such as Poundstretcher, B&M, and The Range.
items.title: Poundland Collapses Into Administration, Putting Over 10,000 Jobs at Risk

items.summary: The Guardian editorial argues that only bold action can win public confidence amid rising UK energy prices, framing the issue around Prime Minister Andy Burnham's focus on the cost of living. Ofgem announced in mid-December that the domestic gas and electricity price cap will rise in January, meaning roughly 22 million households will pay an average equivalent to £2,166 a year for their bills, up from £1,723 under the current cap. The editorial attributes rising costs to international conflict—gas supply volatility linked to uncertainty over the Strait of Hormuz and depleted European reserves following last summer's heatwave—and warns that households may face painful choices between heating and other essentials. It contends this hardship will exhaust the cost of living 'breathing space' already offered by Burnham, consisting of a VAT cut to bills and a one-off £100 payment to some households. The piece criticizes the Conservatives and Reform UK for blaming environmental policies and advocating abandonment of net zero commitments, arguing instead that hastening the transition away from fossil fuels is the strategic route to energy security. It concludes by urging Burnham to deliver on his promised 10-year plan to fix 'broken' markets as he moves beyond breathing space measures.
items.title: UK energy price cap set to rise as cost of living pressures intensify

items.summary: A Delhi court has sent two women accused of participating in the alleged gang-rape of a 22-year-old woman into judicial custody, while a third suspect remains held in police remand. The case stems from an allegation by the survivor, who reportedly works at a cafe in Karkardooma and knew the accused, that she was sexually assaulted after attending a party with them. According to Delhi Police, seven people arrived at a closed cafe in Preet Vihar on Wednesday night; although the establishment had shut at 11:30 pm, one group member allegedly used a key to reopen it for the gathering. The group reportedly consumed alcohol before leaving around 3:30 am, after which the survivor alleged that two men sexually assaulted her and that other members of the group assisted them. Following this complaint, Delhi Police registered a case under sections dealing with gang-rape and arrested three suspects, including the two women now in judicial custody. Police are continuing their search for the remaining individuals allegedly involved while investigating each suspect's role.
items.title: Delhi Court Sends Two Women Accused to Judicial Custody, Third Held in Police Remand

items.summary: Waterleaf (Talinum fruticosum), a staple vegetable in Nigerian dishes such as afang and edikang ikong, has suffered heavy losses across Nigeria since June due to relentless bursts of rain that killed many plants by making their stems brittle or causing leaves to wilt. In Calabar, southeastern Nigeria, women farmers who depend on waterleaf for their livelihoods have largely abandoned crops that failed to survive the rains; some plots around the local airport are described as quiet and lonely. Mongabay fellow Kingsley Charles began covering this slump in September by visiting farms and markets across Calabar and speaking with dozens of farmers, consumers, and vendors about changing rainfall patterns affecting production. While some growers have given up waiting out the rainy season, others like elderly farmer Joy Okon continue to replant—Okon had previously planted roughly eight bags of stem cuttings without success but returned in November to re-stick stems into soil after churning it with a rusted knife and adding manure. Charles's photographs document this food crisis confronting Nigeria's southern coastline as farmers hope for a viable harvest despite the ongoing rains.
items.title: Nigerian Waterleaf Farmers Replant Despite Heavy Rains

items.summary: A fuel-carrying truck reportedly overturned on a busy highway near the Warraq district of Imbaba, a suburb of Cairo, igniting vehicles and prompting a major emergency response. Egyptian Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said at least 30 people were killed and 15 others injured in the Wednesday blaze, which he described as preliminary with the death toll expected to rise further; he also announced his intention to visit the scene. According to state media footage captured by passers-by, a massive fire produced thick smoke while emergency workers pulled victims from burning vehicles amid hundreds of onlookers gathered nearby. Abdel Ghaffar reported that 39 ambulances were dispatched and 15 injured people taken to hospital. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi issued condolences to the victims. The incident comes as traffic accidents continue to claim thousands of lives in Egypt annually, with speeding, poor road conditions, and weak enforcement cited among leading causes; a January multi-vehicle collision near Beni Suef killed 21 people and injured 16.
items.title: At Least 30 Killed in Cairo Highway Fuel-Fire Blast

items.summary: Several automakers are offering discounts of $10,000 or more on select electric vehicles during the upcoming Black Friday shopping period. Kia is providing a $10,000 Customer Cash discount across several models including the EV9 and Niro EV; with that discount applied, the base 2026 EV9 Light RWD trim can fall to as low as $44,900 from its $54,900 starting MSRP. Lucid is offering a $15,000 Black Friday Credit on the new 2027 Gravity Touring and a $10,000 credit on the 2027 Air Touring sedan; both models start at $79,900 with up to 337 miles of range for the Gravity and up to 431 miles for the Air. Lucid's offers end November 30, Kia's deals run until January 4, 2027, and Volkswagen's offer runs until November 30, 2026.
items.title: Kia, Lucid and Volkswagen Offer EV Discounts of $10,000 or More for Black Friday

items.summary: Crude oil prices fell this week as traders leaned into a predicted supply glut, but the article argues that growing tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz contradict that narrative. Kpler reported that by October 8, daily traffic through the strait had fallen to its lowest since July at about 10.1 million barrels per day—back to September averages but only 74% of pre-war levels—and then continued sliding after a mid-October wartime high above 20 million barrels: down to 16.03 million in late October, 15.77 million for the first week of November, and 13.96 million for the second week of that month. Meanwhile, attacks on tankers have become routine; Reuters' Clyde Russell cited Kpler data showing 12 tanker attacks since early November after 17 in October, while three vessels were damaged by mines or unidentified projectiles at the start of this week alone. The article notes that Middle East export volumes are trending lower as vessel attacks trend higher, and points to other risks—China's Sinopec buying about 20 million barrels from West Africa since monthstart (roughly a full typical-month Chinese West African total), record Russian oil imports by India and China, Iraq's dispute with the Kurdistan government over northern fields, and Houthi strikes on Saudi energy targets. The piece concludes that traders appear to be ignoring this data while clinging to the assumption of an irreversible September rebound and imminent peace—underscued by President Trump's suggestion to Fox News that the U.S. could resume attacks on Iranian targets in 2027.
items.title: Oil Traders Ignore Growing Threat to Persian Gulf Supply

items.summary: A fuel tanker crash ignited a large fire on Egypt's Ring Road near the Waraq neighborhood of Giza in Greater Cairo, Egyptian authorities said Wednesday. The blaze killed at least 30 people and injured at least 25 others (Public Prosecutor's office), while leaving more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred. Rescue workers pulled survivors from burning vehicles as firefighters battled the spreading flames near Imbaba, a Cairo suburb. President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi issued condolences to victims' families, and DNA investigations were underway to identify them. Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said injured people had been taken to nearby hospitals and that he would travel to the scene; he described the death toll as preliminary, raising concerns it could rise further.

items.summary: Following intelligence reports shared among NATO allies that Russia is preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite within 60 days, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has promised the alliance will defend against any threats in space. The potential launch prompted Jamie Shea, former NATO spokesperson, to join Euronews' Europe Tonight program to discuss how satellite systems could be affected and what such an event would mean for the world, including lessons learned from past nuclear detonations in space.
items.title: NATO Vows Space Defense After Reports Russia Prepares Nuclear Satellite Launch

items.summary: Ukrainian forces have executed a series of successful strikes against Russian assets worldwide, disabling a cargo vessel off Finland and sinking the corvette Merkury while damaging another ship in Libyan waters. The article frames these attacks as evidence that the war has officially gone global, though it notes this international dimension predates 2022 — Ukraine's allies have supplied aid since Russia's full-fledged invasion in 2022, providing critical air defense and economic support despite disruptions from U.S. President Donald Trump's involvement in negotiations. The conflict remains at an equilibrium with no decisive breakthrough likely; the year 2026 has not advanced Ukraine's goal of ending the war amid a stagnant front, increased Russian aerial attacks, and a recalcitrant American president. Russia has also suffered heavily, with more than 400,000 Russians killed in the war — potentially as many as 700,000. The piece argues that because neither side can produce needed armaments alone in this industrialized conflict of attrition, both must target their adversary's international allies; Ukraine has focused on delegitimizing Russia's narratives and striking Russian assets abroad to pressure Vladimir Putin's government.
items.title: Recent Sinking of Russian Vessels Abroad Signals the Russia-Ukraine War Has Gone Global

items.summary: Threat actors are chaining the PHP2Shell and Fragnesia vulnerabilities to attack Palo Alto Networks devices whose management interfaces face the public internet. The attacks combine CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (PHP2Shell), which let unauthenticated attackers run code with PHP web worker privileges, with CVE-2026-46300 (Fragnesia), a Linux kernel flaw in the XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem that lets a low-privilege local attacker escalate to root. A CISA alert on October 28 warned both issues were being chained to deploy PHP webshells and run commands as root, and Dream Security researchers reported observing the same campaign targeting servers in the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, including a U.S. government affiliate. Palo Alto Networks confirmed today that exploitation of CVE-2026-46300 has been observed against its PAN-OS management interface exposed to the internet, noting all activity it saw involved devices violating recommended best practices by exposing their management interfaces publicly; the company did not provide technical details on how PHP2Shell is chained but said this is the only known exploitation pathway for Fragnesia. Fixes were released for PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1, and 12.2 (with patch-carrying builds varying by release), so administrators who applied PHP2Shell updates should be safe from these attacks; the company also recommends restricting remote management access to trusted internal IP addresses.
items.title: Palo Alto Networks Confirms Fragnesia Flaw Exploited Against PAN-OS Devices

items.summary: After years of hype and few commercial deployments worldwide, small modular reactors (SMRs) are gaining real momentum in the United States through a series of recent milestones. SMRs are factory-built nuclear units that are cheaper than traditional large-scale plants—which have seen only one new U.S. plant added to the grid over the past decade—and safer with smaller land footprints, making them competitive against wind and solar amid those sources' expansion roadblocks. Despite this appeal, commercial deployment has lagged: Oilprice.com reported in June that many hurdles remain after companies presented prototypes and lab results, noting that over 120 distinct SMR designs have been recorded globally compared to 83 in 2022 (q1=120 distinct; q2=83), though most designs still lack licensing. Momentum has since accelerated: at the end of September, the Tennessee Valley Authority became the first U.S. utility authorized to build a commercial SMR using GE Vernova Hitachi's BWRX-300 reactor (the second-ever domestic construction authorization). This week, an engineering alliance between Sargent & Lundy and ENTRA1 Energy announced plans to deploy scalable SMR plants globally using NuScale's certified reactors—the only proprietary design approved by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission—moving these units from theory into real-world deployment.
items.title: U.S. Small Modular Reactors Gain Momentum After Years of Delay

items.summary: In an interview with EL PAÍS conducted in a Mexico City hotel during an academic event, Cuban journalist Abraham Jiménez Enoa discussed his difficult process of talking about Cuba again after being imprisoned for journalism as a founder of the independent magazine El Estornudo. He recounted how State Security agents forced him to undress inside a prison cell and broadcasted his interrogation on state television, turning him into a pariah despite his family's revolutionary ties—his grandmother was a former bodyguard of Fidel Castro and Che Guevara—and prompting his January 2022 exile to Barcelona. Jiménez described the experience as a love-hate relationship that initially bred repulsion toward Cuban accents but eventually led to reconciliation when he began crying over a Carlos Varela song, while also noting how leaving Cuba made him colder and more reclusive than before. He characterized himself as an exile rather than a migrant because he was forced out, explaining the resulting permanent existential dissociation where his body is in Barcelona but his mind remains elsewhere. Jiménez said that State Security harassment caused deep depression and that admitting to being broken by persecution felt powerful and honest, while family breakups over revolutionary versus dissident divides left him unable to reconcile with relatives like his father, who had a stroke. He expressed frustration at non-Cubans voicing opinions about Cuba in Spain, which he considered an insult, and observed that the Spanish far-right party Vox and mainstream conservative PP welcome Cuban dissidents while the left fails to acknowledge human rights abuses on the island. Jiménez described visiting Miami for the first time in 2024 as a trip to the past filled with Trump flags and ICE-style harassment of immigrants, concluding that Florida's exiles have 'a Fidel Castro inside of them.' He also voiced fear about Vox potentially governing Spain due to threats against his Black daughter, who is one of few Black students at her school, while noting he would do anything for her even if it meant leaving Spain.
items.title: Cuban Exile Abraham Jiménez on Florida's Far-Right Dissidents and Spain's Racial Threats

items.summary: An explosion at the Habas Group steel factory in Aliaga, near Izmir, on November 9 killed 19 people (with one missing presumed dead), occurring during a boiler replacement operation when an overhead crane collapsed inside a furnace. The Health and Safety Labour Watch observatory recorded at least 2,014 workplace deaths since January 2026 by November 13 — noting the state undercounts because it excludes refugees, suicides, and child labour from official tallies. Asli Odman of that observatory stated at least 2,000 people die each year directly from workplace accidents in Turkey (per the observatory), a figure she said does not include an estimated 15,000 to 20,000 deaths from occupational diseases — which official government figures put at zero as of 2025. The International Labour Organisation recorded 11.5 workplace deaths per 100,000 workers in Turkey in 2024, the second-highest rate globally that year behind only South Africa. Odman argued that investing in safety costs more than letting people die because it is cheaper for companies to let workers be killed at work. The Habas Group has a history of incidents: a subcontractor died from a fall on October 21 and another was killed by an explosion inflating a tyre on November 5, while the factory reportedly never shut down after this blast. Separately, in May 2026 Mehmet Rustu Başaran, chairman of Habas Group, and other executives were sentenced to more than four years in prison for negligence following a 2017 LPG tanker explosion in Kocaeli that killed one person. Nine people are now in custody (two under house arrest, including the Habas chairman) as part of the public prosecutor's investigation into this November 9 blast.
items.title: Turkey's Aliaga steel factory blast killed 19, exposing systemic workplace safety failures

items.summary: Toyota is set to reveal its first extended-range electric vehicle (EREV) on November 27 at the Guangzhou Motor Show through its China joint venture GAC Toyota. The EREV uses a gas engine as a generator to recharge a smaller battery when it runs low, extending range while typically being quieter and cheaper than a plug-in hybrid but less efficient than a pure EV. Based on the first preview image—which resembles the Highlander—and translated text reading “Cash in on the classics. Global flagship SUV. Not a quick fix, but a range extender,” all signs point to it being an extended-range version of the Highlander, though Toyota has not confirmed the name or details; GAC Toyota’s Weibo caption read #Toyota doesn’t rush but range-extended. The debut follows September Nikkei reporting that production would begin in China in spring 2027, and Toyota aims to produce about 200,000 EREVs in 2027 with output roughly doubling to around 400,000 units in 2028. Separately, the fully electric three-row Highlander BEV will launch in early 2027 without a US version; it offers front- and all-wheel-drive options with two battery packs—77 kWh or 95.8 kWh—with up to 287 miles of range for the smaller pack and up to 320 miles for the larger pack in FWD models, seating seven passengers, and will be built at Toyota’s Georgetown, Kentucky plant.

items.summary: In Liberia, families celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving on the first Thursday in November, a tradition brought by Black American settlers from the American Colonization Society when they founded the community that grew into the country. The holiday dates to the first half of the 19th century and has evolved over time in response to national events: after Britain continued trying to seize Liberian territory following independence in 1847, President Alfred Francis Russell called on God for protection against the intruders in 1883, and that same year the legislature officially established Thanksgiving as a national holiday rooted in religious gratitude. Yvonne Capehart Weah, from Caldwell township, describes it as giving thanks to God for freedom, divine protection, unity, and the harvest; her family gathers outside under trees because so many relatives attend they cannot fit around a dining table, beginning their celebration at morning church service. The holiday is observed by people of all faiths: Muslims pray in mosques while Christians go to church, and YouTuber Sekou Muhammad Sheriff notes that as a boy his father bought him a shirt-trouser suit with slippers for the day. Unlike American Thanksgiving, Liberian celebrations do not feature turkey; instead families serve fried, smoked, or roasted chicken along with jollof rice, watermelon, pineapple, stews including one made from sweet potato leaves and another called king's meat featuring snails, and fufu and soup of cassava, fish, chicken, okra, and chili pepper. Sheriff did not host Thanksgiving this year due to lack of resources but remains thankful for his health and for Liberia's peace after civil conflicts between 1989 and 1997 and again from 1999 to 2003.
items.title: How American Thanksgiving took root and evolved in Liberia

items.summary: 1Password disclosed a data breach after an employee's corporate GitHub account was hacked and used to deploy malicious code into the company's backend services, which downloaded customer records. The investigation began on November 19 when indications of the compromised account were detected. Stolen customer data included names, email addresses, account and user IDs, creation and last sign-in timestamps, public cryptographic keys, SRP protocol parameters, invitation/provisioning/recovery tokens, and other internal metadata; the attacker also accessed private source code repositories and the CI/CD environment, potentially exposing internal infrastructure credentials. 1Password states that customer password vaults and the encryption keys protecting them were not compromised. The stolen recovery and provisioning tokens cannot be used alone to access accounts because completing an invitation or recovery requires either single sign-on authentication or a six-digit verification code sent by email; as a precaution against brute-force attacks, these codes have been strengthened from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric characters. 1Password has disabled the compromised GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, restored clean versions of affected services, and rotated or revoked potentially exposed infrastructure credentials, while hiring independent cybersecurity experts who found no internal evidence of customer account takeovers. The company is not requiring customers to change passwords or Secret Keys but warns them about phishing attempts impersonating 1Password that could lure users into disclosing their credentials.
items.title: 1Password Data Breach After Employee GitHub Account Compromised
